html:
Cochinchina is the European name for southern Vietnam: the Mekong delta and the city of Saigon. It was Khmer land until the 1600s, when the Nguyễn lords, who ruled the south of a divided Vietnam, pushed into it. Vietnamese settlers, and Chinese refugees loyal to the fallen Ming, cleared the delta, and the Nguyễn set up a province at Saigon in 1698.

The map shows it from 1783 to 1815, the years of the Tây Sơn wars. Nguyễn Ánh, a surviving Nguyễn prince, used Saigon as his base, got help from the French bishop Pigneau de Behaine, and in 1802 became emperor of all Vietnam as Gia Long.

It reappears from 1920 to 1945 as a French colony. France took it in the Cochinchina campaign of 1858 to 1867 and, unlike Annam and Tonkin, ruled it directly. It was part of French Indochina. The delta became a huge exporter of rice, and rubber plantations spread inland. New religions grew here: Caodaism in 1926 and Hòa Hảo in 1939. In 1949 it joined the new State of Vietnam.
